# Key assumptions check on the article's diagnosis and point of view

## Scope and method

The brief asks whether the article accurately diagnoses its phenomenon (organisations measure AI transformation by adoption, and adoption measures miss workarounds and value) and whether its point of view is valid. The favoured reading, taken from the seven earlier results, is this: the narrow diagnosis follows from how a usage count works; the claims about how common the phenomenon is are asserted and not shown; and the wider conclusions (that every workaround shows design failure, that nobody adopts AI, that tiered reporting is the fix) are less well supported than the narrow diagnosis.

This check lists the premises that the favoured reading needs to be true, in two groups. Part A covers the article's own premises. Part B covers the premises inside the earlier findings, because a check of the findings has to test what they take for granted as well as what the article does. Each premise is marked stated or unstated, and challenged, then kept or dropped. Each kept premise has the conditions that would show it false. The article gives almost no conditions of its own, so the conditions below are my constructions from the material and the findings, and they are labelled as such.

The article has no item numbers. Quotations are copied exactly from the article. The material is one article of unknown date and publisher, supplied as text, so nothing outside the article was checked. Findings that mention E1, E2, E3 and E4 are cited as the earlier results reported them, and I could not check those summaries.

## Part A: premises in the article

### A1. Organisations mostly report adoption as their measure of AI progress

- Origin: stated, with one hedge. "Adoption seems to have gone mainstream as the way organisations describe their progress with AI".
- Challenge: this is the factual premise of the whole diagnosis. No organisation, survey or count supports it, and the article does not say what share of programs also report outcome measures.
- Status: kept, marked vulnerable.
- Invalidating condition (mine): evidence that most programs report outcome or quality measures next to usage, in which case the article argues against a narrower practice than it describes.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A2. Programs report adoption because it can be counted early, and vendors and consultancies follow

- Origin: stated. "So AI programs report adoption instead, because it can be counted from the first week of a rollout." Also "Following their lead, vendors set their pricing based on seats and usage, and consultancies build their frameworks around it."
- Challenge: the first sentence names one cause. A second cause, that seat and usage data come with the vendor's product and cost nothing to collect, fits the text equally well and reverses the direction of influence. The article does not choose between them.
- Status: kept for the claim that adoption is cheap and early; dropped for the claim about who leads whom, because nothing supports it and the diagnosis does not need it.
- Invalidating condition (mine): evidence that vendor reporting tools came first and programs adopted what was supplied.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A3. A count of use cannot tell designed use from a workaround

- Origin: stated. "A workaround does not show up as non-use."
- Challenge: this holds for the usage figures the article defines (people using an app, frequency of AI feature use, tokens consumed). It does not hold automatically for every dashboard a real organisation runs. The earlier results accept it as true by logic. That is correct for the article's definition and untested for real telemetry, which may include completion, error or support-contact data.
- Status: kept. This is the best supported premise in the article.
- Invalidating condition (mine): usage reporting that is routinely read together with task completion, time per task or support requests, so that workarounds leave a visible trace.
- Stated invalidating condition: none. The article does not consider richer usage data.

### A4. Workarounds are common enough, and large enough in effect, to make adoption figures misleading

- Origin: unstated. The article gives examples of workarounds at five levels and no frequency for any.
- Challenge: the diagnosis needs workarounds to be frequent, because a rare behaviour would not make a count misleading. The article shows that workarounds can exist. It does not show that they are widespread.
- Status: kept as needed for the diagnosis, marked vulnerable, and named below as a likely point of error.
- Invalidating condition (mine): observation across several programs in which workarounds are rare, or in which usage figures track outcomes closely.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A5. The workaround examples were observed

- Origin: stated by assertion. "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation."
- Challenge: no study, sample, setting or date is named. The five-level typology and the task example about editing records depend on this one sentence. It cannot be confirmed or refuted from the material.
- Status: kept provisionally, as an illustration of a mechanism and not as evidence of frequency.
- Invalidating condition (mine): the research does not exist, or the examples came from a single setting that is atypical.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A6. A person either uses a tool as designed or works around it

- Origin: stated. "Faced with any tool at work, a person does one of two things. They use it as designed, or they find a workaround that gets the job done."
- Challenge: the split leaves out partial use, mixed use, plain non-use and abandonment. It matters because abandonment is the case usage counts do see, so the split narrows the cases to those that favour the argument.
- Status: dropped in its absolute form. Kept as a simplification for the typology, with the consequence that the diagnosis covers the cases where use is recorded and the work is done another way, and not all poor outcomes.
- Invalidating condition (mine): any observed pattern that is neither designed use nor a successful workaround, which is easy to find.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A7. Adoption, properly understood, means effective use as designed

- Origin: stated. "If adoption means anything at work, it means the tool works well enough, as designed, for people to get the job done with it. A workaround is its opposite."
- Challenge: with this definition, adoption excludes workarounds by construction, so "adoption measures miss workarounds" is partly true by definition. The earlier results say this in two places (FQ-03 and TC1-21) and count it both as support and as a defect. It is neither on its own. It makes the narrow claim safe from refutation and moves the empirical question to A4.
- Status: kept as a stipulation the author is entitled to make, with the cost that the claim then says less about the world than it appears to.
- Invalidating condition (mine): the article uses "adoption" in the counting sense elsewhere in the same argument without saying so, which it does ("adoption is itself a workaround", and the title).
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A8. Adoption programs depend on a literal meaning of "adopt AI"

- Origin: stated. "AI adoption assumes that people actually "adopt AI". Taken literally, they do not."
- Challenge: the article itself describes adoption as a habit "borrowed from earlier software rollouts, where success meant getting people to use the new system", which is an ordinary organisational sense and not a literal one. Nothing in the diagnosis needs the literal reading.
- Status: dropped as a premise of the diagnosis. The earlier results differ on how much this matters: TC1-19 calls Argument 4 the weakest link, and FQ-03 says the article's point "stands without this step". Both are correct. The premise is not needed for the diagnosis, and it is needed only for the recommendation to stop organising programs around adopting AI.
- Invalidating condition (mine): programs that use the word loosely, which the article concedes.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A9. AI is becoming a component of every tool, as web search did

- Origin: stated as present fact. "A program built around adopting AI is organised around a technology that is becoming a component of everything."
- Challenge: this is a prediction supported by one past case, and it covers only the article's first case (a tool with AI inside). The second case, a person who learns a new job because agents do part of the work, is not a component becoming ordinary. The article also says "AI is not a single thing that a person chooses and takes responsibility for", and gives no ground for that against standalone assistants that people do choose and answer for.
- Status: kept, marked vulnerable.
- Invalidating condition (mine): AI products that stay separate and are chosen deliberately by staff, which is the way many organisations currently buy them.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A10. Every workaround shows where the design failed

- Origin: stated. "Each workaround shows which part of the design failed, for whom, and what people do instead."
- Challenge: the article's own team example (no time to train) and leadership example (a manager shaping recorded usage) come from workload and incentives, and its remedies for them are training time and a statement on how figures will be used. The claim is secure for interface, task and workflow cases. The article gives one conditional limit: "Training people to use the tool as designed will not help when the design is the reason they work around it." That limit is about training and does not extend the claim to the other causes.
- Status: kept only in a wider form ("design of the tool, the work and the incentives"), which the article does not state. Dropped as written.
- Invalidating condition (mine): any workaround traced to skill, preference or an unsafe shortcut and not to a design fault.
- Stated invalidating condition: partial (the training limit above).

### A11. Programs blame people because they have no evidence about design

- Origin: stated. "A program measured by adoption rates cannot see workarounds, so when the work does not improve it has no evidence about the design and looks for the cause in people instead."
- Challenge: this is a causal story about program behaviour with no case behind it. It also treats "the organisation did not follow the program" as a claim about people, when it may be a claim about the program. Other causes of poor results, such as a tool that performs badly or a task that AI does not help, are not considered.
- Status: kept as plausible, marked vulnerable.
- Invalidating condition (mine): programs that measure by adoption and still examine design through support tickets, complaints or user research.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A12. Removed work cannot be recorded by an adoption measure, and this is the largest gap

- Origin: stated. "An adoption measure has no way to record this value." and "The largest gap is value that adoption cannot see at all."
- Challenge: the first claim follows for usage counts. The second is a comparison supported by two hypothetical examples. The article says "there is no earlier version of the work to compare it with", yet its medium-term tier compares against "how it was done before". A baseline for removed work may exist in the earlier volume of requests or checks, which the article does not mention. The earlier results disagree on whether this is a contradiction or a difference of scale (TC1-19 offers the scale reading as an alternative). The text supports either reading.
- Status: kept for usage counts. Dropped as "cannot be measured at all", and unproven as "largest".
- Invalidating condition (mine): an organisation that records the earlier volume of the removed work and shows the change.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A13. A count of workarounds found and removed is a valid early sign of value

- Origin: unstated. The text says only "Workarounds found and removed can be reported from the first weeks of a rollout, which is when adoption figures are reported now."
- Challenge: this is the step that links the diagnosis to the remedy. Fewer workarounds could mean a better tool, or staff who have learned not to show them, which is the pattern the article describes for usage figures. The article proposes a new measure that is easy to report early, after faulting adoption for that quality.
- Status: kept as needed for the remedy, marked vulnerable, and named below as a likely point of error.
- Invalidating condition (mine): a program in which workaround counts fell while outcomes did not improve.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A14. Observation and questioning will reveal workarounds

- Origin: unstated.
- Challenge: the team and leadership examples describe people hiding or shaping their use, so candour cannot be assumed. The leadership fix (a statement of how figures will be used) addresses this, but the short-term tier does not say how observation avoids the same distortion. The cost of observing work is also not discussed, while the article says adoption is used because it "can be counted from the first week".
- Status: kept, marked vulnerable.
- Invalidating condition (mine): observers finding fewer workarounds where staff fear consequences than where they do not.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A15. People who work around a tool have judged the situation correctly

- Origin: unstated. It sits behind the advice that task workarounds need "checks that ask for real judgement, not approval", which follows the example of staff editing records so a review does not trigger.
- Challenge: "responsible for getting the work done" does not show that they were right to skip the review. The example could be a poor review step or a removed control, and the article does not say how to tell them apart.
- Status: kept, marked vulnerable.
- Invalidating condition (mine): a case where the skipped review would have caught an error.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

### A16. Established methods will work for this kind of change

- Origin: stated. "These principles were true before AI and are still true now."
- Challenge: the article also says AI is changing work "in ways that are hard to picture in advance". TC1-13 notes that the one historical case it examined was inconclusive for years and gives no support for expecting quick results from older methods. The appeal rests on the claim being obvious.
- Status: kept as a reason the proposal is low risk, dropped as a reason it will work.
- Invalidating condition (mine): a type of AI-driven change for which observation, outcome design and role design have been tried and failed.
- Stated invalidating condition: none.

## Part B: premises inside the earlier findings

### B1. The narrow diagnosis is sound because it follows from logic

- Origin: unstated in the findings, but common to FQ-03, TC1-19, TC1-21, DM-07 and CM1-14.
- Challenge: this is A3 and A7 restated. The soundness depends on the article's own narrow definitions of usage figures and of adoption. Under those definitions it is close to true by construction. Under a looser definition of either term, it becomes an empirical claim that the material cannot test.
- Status: kept, with that dependence added to the favoured reading.
- Invalidating condition: either definition changes, or real reporting practice is shown to differ from the article's description.

### B2. Agreement across the findings is independent confirmation

- Origin: unstated.
- Challenge: the seven results reach the same few conclusions (unsourced premise, team and leadership examples not design faults, tension between removed work and the medium-term tier, no evidence for the tiers). They were all produced from the same article, and several use each other's readings of the same passages. The repeated points are closer to one observation seen from several angles than to seven separate tests. The same applies to the five inconsistencies counted against H1 in DM-07, which that result itself says are of one kind.
- Status: kept with reduced weight. The agreement shows the points are visible in the text. It does not show they are correct.
- Invalidating condition: the same conclusions can be reached by a method that does not use the article's wording, which none of the seven results did.

### B3. Missing sources count against the article

- Origin: unstated, and handled in two ways. Every result lists the absence of sources as a defect, and every result also lists genre (a short opinion piece) as an alternative explanation.
- Challenge: the brief asks whether claims are supported by the article's "own evidence", so absence of support is a fair finding whatever the genre. Absence of support does not show a claim is false. The findings sometimes slide from "unsupported" to "doubtful".
- Status: kept in the form "unsupported, not shown wrong".
- Invalidating condition: the research cited in the sentence "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation." is produced and bears out the examples.

### B4. H2 is the best reading because it has the fewest inconsistencies

- Origin: stated in DM-07.
- Challenge: DM-07 itself says H2 is rated consistent on every item, which makes it the broadest and hardest to refute. "Partly supported, but asserts more than it shows" would fit nearly any opinion article. Its zero count reflects its breadth as much as its fit. The firm result in that matrix is only that H1 (fully supported) is not credible, and that rests on missing-evidence items.
- Status: kept as a modest reading. It is not strong evidence that the article is more or less accurate than average.
- Invalidating condition: a narrower version of H2 that makes a testable claim, such as a stated share of workarounds, and is scored against the material.

### B5. Evidence from outside the article bears on the article's own evidence

- Origin: unstated. TC1-13 and DM-07 use E1 (a trial) and E2 (a vendor survey), and TC1-13 says E3 and E4 were read only as summaries.
- Challenge: E1 and E2 are not cited by the article, so they cannot show that the article is supported by its own evidence. Both findings say as much, and E2 is rated by DM-07 as a vendor survey that does not confirm anything. Even so, the results use them to colour conclusions, such as the 78% figure that "is consistent with" the personal-tool example. I could not see these sources and have not relied on them.
- Status: kept only as context. Dropped as support for or against the article's own claims.
- Invalidating condition: the sources are read in full and found to measure the behaviours the article describes.

### B6. The team and leadership examples fall outside "design failure"

- Origin: stated in FQ-03, TC1-19, TC1-21, CM1-01 and CM1-14.
- Challenge: this depends on reading "design" as tool design. The article's own workflow experience idea covers which steps are automated, what passes at each handover and who is accountable, which is wider. FQ-03 and TC1-19 both give the wider reading as an alternative. The article's heading is ambiguous and does not state which it means.
- Status: kept as a finding about wording, dropped as a finding about reasoning. The article should say which meaning it intends.
- Invalidating condition: the author states that "design" includes workload and incentives.

## Likely points of error

These are the kept premises for which the article states no condition that would show them false, and which the diagnosis or the remedy needs. They are listed in order of how much of the argument depends on them.

1. A1, that organisations mostly report adoption. The whole diagnosis starts here and no support is given.
2. A4, that workarounds are common enough to matter. The article proves existence and not frequency.
3. A13, that a count of workarounds found and removed is a valid early sign of value. This is the unstated link between diagnosis and remedy, and it is open to the concealment problem the article raises itself.
4. A14, that observation will reveal workarounds in settings where the article says people hide them.
5. A10 and A11, that every workaround is a design failure and that programs blame people for lack of design evidence. Both are causal claims with no case behind them, and the article's own examples go against the first.
6. A9, that AI is becoming a component of everything. It is a prediction stated as present fact.

Premises that are safer: A3 (a usage count does not record how work was done) and A7 as a stipulation. Their safety comes from definitions, so they say less about practice than they appear to.

## What this means for the favoured reading

The favoured reading survives with three changes. First, the narrow diagnosis is sound mainly because the article defines usage figures and adoption in a way that makes it so. Second, the seven results agree more than they independently confirm, so the weight of the agreement should be lowered. Third, the weakest part of the point of view is the remedy, because the unstated premises A13 and A14 connect it to the diagnosis and the article gives no condition under which they would fail. The article's claims about prevalence are unsupported and should be treated as untested, not as wrong.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The premise list is my reconstruction. A different reader could split the article's claims differently, for example treating A10 and A11 as one premise.
- Marking a premise "vulnerable" is a judgement about how much support the material gives it. It is not a measure of how likely the premise is to be false.
- The invalidating conditions are mine, because the article states almost none. They are plausible tests and not tests the author accepts.
- Part B depends on reading the seven earlier results as written. I did not re-run their methods, and I could not check E1 to E4, which they cite as summaries.
- The material is one article with no source, date or publisher, and it was supplied as text, so it may differ from the published page.
- This check cannot say whether the phenomenon is real. It lists what must be true for the favoured reading to hold.
- No counting or code was needed for this technique.

## Alternative explanations

- The article may be written as a practitioner's framework and not as a study. On that reading the missing sources and conditions are a choice of form, and the unstated premises (A4, A13, A14) are the author's experience, which the reader is asked to test against their own. The material cannot tell an unreported study from an unsupported assertion.
- The wide use of "design" and "adoption" may be deliberate. If the author means design to include workload and incentives, and adoption to mean effective use, then A7, A10 and B6 are consistent, and the problems found are problems of stated definitions and not of reasoning.
- The tension between removed work and the medium-term comparison may be sequencing and scale. The article may intend removed work to be handled only by the end-state tier, which would make A12 consistent with the remedy.
- The agreement across the findings (B2) may reflect that the article has a small number of clear weaknesses, so several methods reach the same ones. On that reading the agreement is more informative than I have allowed.
- The favoured reading may be too cautious. If the readers the article is written for already know that workarounds are common, the narrow diagnosis needs no frequency evidence, and the gaps in A1 and A4 matter less.

# Historical analogy: AI adoption measures and the IT productivity paradox

## Purpose and cases

The brief asks whether the article diagnoses its phenomenon accurately and whether its point of view is valid. This technique tests one part of that: whether the past case offered by the evidence folder (the productivity paradox of information technology, E3) is a fair guide to the present case, and what it does and does not tell us about the article's claims. The article itself does not cite the paradox. It reasons by its own analogies (ecommerce, the cloud, web search) and ends by saying "we've done this before with methods that still work". The comparison below is therefore my construction, not the article's argument.

Past case (E3): Brynjolfsson's 1993 review in Communications of the ACM. As recorded in the material, it "found that earlier studies generally did not identify significant productivity gains, and it judged that the evidence was inconclusive, partly because productivity from IT was almost impossible to assess with the measures then available." A later paper (Brynjolfsson and Hitt, 1998) "reported positive results from new data." E3 was read only as a search summary (abstract and introduction), so the mechanism behind the outcome is known at the level of "measures were inadequate", not in detail.

Present case, stated as the technique requires:

- Known (from the article): organisations report adoption (users, frequency, tokens) as progress. The article says this is because value "does not show up quickly in financial results". Vendor pricing and consultancy frameworks are said to follow adoption.
- Known (from E1 and E2, as evidence about the present only): E1 is a randomised trial of 16 experienced developers on 246 tasks. Tasks took 19% longer with AI allowed, yet developers afterwards believed AI had cut time by 20%. E2 is a Microsoft and LinkedIn survey: 78% of AI users bring their own AI tools to work, 39% have received company AI training, and 53% worry that revealing AI use signals they are replaceable.
- Unclear: how widespread workarounds are, how much value is of the "removes the need for the work" kind, and whether usage figures correlate with outcomes at all. The article gives no counts.
- Presumed by the article: that adoption is the main measure in use, that workarounds are common and invisible to usage data, and that the listed workarounds were observed. The article states "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation" but names no study, sample or date.

## Likenesses and differences

Ratings: strong, moderate, weak, not analogous. The "check against mechanism" column states what produced the earlier outcome in E3 and whether the element holds for the present case.

| # | Element | Past case (E3) | Present case | Check against the mechanism of the past outcome | Rating |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Expected benefit is hard to see in outcome figures | Studies did not find significant productivity gains | Article: neither cost reduction nor productivity "shows up quickly in financial results" | The paradox arose because gains were absent from, or not detectable in, the measures. The article makes the same claim about time lag and traceability. Same mechanism, though the article gives no data of its own. | Strong |
| 2 | Cause attributed to the measures, not only to the technology | Evidence inconclusive "partly because" productivity was almost impossible to assess with then-available measures | Article: adoption measures "cannot show" whether work is better, faster or more reliable | Both place at least part of the cause in the measurement instrument. E3 says "partly", so the lesson supports "measures are a contributing problem", not "measures are the problem". | Strong |
| 3 | What the measure counts | Aggregate productivity and output statistics | Usage counts (users, frequency, tokens) | Different failure. The past measures tried to capture output and were too coarse. Adoption measures do not try to capture output at all; they count inputs. The paradox lesson (better outcome data was needed) transfers, but the specific defect differs. | Moderate |

It does not show that the article's tiers are the right data, and E3 gives no detail on what the new data were. | Moderate |

It shows that self-reported and perceived benefit can diverge from measured outcomes, which supports distrust of proxies. It does not show workarounds, and E1 covers 16 developers in one task type with early-2025 tools. | Weak (as support for the article's diagnosis) |

E1 is consistent with use and effectiveness separating but does not measure tokens or attempts. Untested in the material. | Weak |

E2's 53% worry about being seen as replaceable is consistent with leadership and team concealment, but it is a vendor survey whose method was not read, and it concerns worry, not behaviour. | Weak |

The article's closing claim is only partly supported: the observation and design practices it lists are not the measures that failed in E3, so the two do not conflict directly, but E3 gives no support for confidence that they work quickly. | Weak |

## Where the cases correspond (lessons that can be applied)

- Elements 1, 2 and 5. When a technology's benefit is not visible in outcome data, the cause may be partly the measures and partly a time lag. This supports the article's diagnosis that early reporting by adoption stands in for value that cannot yet be seen. It supports "partly", which is what E3 says.
- Element 4 (moderate). Better data later changed the finding in the past case, so an argument for improving the evidence is reasonable.

## Where the cases diverge (lessons that must not be applied)

- Elements 6, 9 and 11. E3 does not contain anything about workarounds, concealment or value from removed work. These parts of the article's diagnosis cannot be said to be supported by the past case. They rest on the article's reasoning and on the unnamed "actual observations".
- Element 3. The past measurement failure was too coarse an output measure. The present one, on the article's account, is a use measure standing in for outcomes. A fix suited to the first (more precise output data) is not the same as the article's fix (observe workarounds, then track outcomes).
- Element 12. The past case should not be used to claim that existing methods will resolve this quickly.

## What this means for the brief

On the part of the diagnosis that the past case can test (adoption or similar proxies reported because outcomes are hard to measure; measures are part of the problem; evidence improves later), the diagnosis is supported by analogy, though E3 was read only as a summary. On the part that is central to the article's point of view (workarounds hide behind usage figures, and the design is at fault), the analogy gives no support, and the evidence in the material is thin. E2's 78% bring-your-own-tools figure is consistent with the interface and task workaround of using a personal tool, but it is a vendor survey with unread method and it does not measure workarounds inside approved tools. E1 supports caution about perceived benefit but is narrow.

Claims the article makes without support in its own text: the statement that the listed workarounds are "actual observations from research" (no source), that adoption "seems to have gone mainstream" (no count), and that vendors and consultancies follow adoption (no examples). The article's reasoning is mostly sound where it is logical (use and effective work can diverge; a workaround can look like active use). It leaves out any estimate of how often these occur, any case where high adoption did coincide with good outcomes, and any alternative reason for non-improvement, such as a tool that is poorly suited to the task for reasons other than interface design, which it partly acknowledges when it lists data quality and trust.

## Assumptions and limitations

- Assumed that the productivity paradox is a reasonable past case. It was chosen by the brief, not tested against other candidates, so the fit test's concern about testing only one analogy applies. The result cannot say whether another case (for example earlier enterprise software rollouts, which the article mentions) would give different lessons.
- E3 was available only as a search summary of the abstract and introduction. The mechanism of the earlier outcome is therefore stated at a high level, and the 1998 reversal is one sentence with no detail on what changed.
- E1 and E2 were also search summaries. E2 is a vendor survey whose method was not read. E1 is a trial with 16 developers.
- The article gives no dates, publisher or sources, and the supplied text could not be checked against the original page.
- The technique compares topics; it cannot verify the article's claims about workarounds, which need observation data that the material does not hold.
- Ratings are my judgement on the material, not measured.

## Alternative explanations

- The strong correspondence on elements 1 and 2 may reflect only that any new technology has lagged and hard-to-measure benefits. If so, the paradox supports patience, not the article's specific view that adoption metrics are a distinct error.
- The article's diagnosis may be accurate in direction but its attribution of non-improvement to design failure may be too narrow. The same observed gaps between usage and results could come from tools that perform poorly (as E1 suggests for one task type), from tasks where AI does not help, or from lack of training (E2: 39% trained), none of which is a workaround.
- Adoption figures may be reported not because organisations cannot think of better measures but because they are cheap and early. That would make the issue one of incentives, not of an incorrect concept, and would weaken the article's claim that the problem lies in the basic concept of adoption.

# Absence analysis of "Adopt an AI, today: a workaround for measuring AI transformation"

## Scope and method

The claim tested is the article's diagnosis: organisations measure AI transformation by adoption, and adoption measures miss workarounds and value. The reference structure is the DeLone and McLean model (E4), which has six dimensions (information quality, system quality, service quality, use, user satisfaction, net benefits) and keeps use separate from net benefits. A discussion of measuring AI success that was complete against this model would be expected to touch each dimension. I also list items that any argument resting on an empirical diagnosis would be expected to contain, whatever the model says.

I counted terms in the article text (about 2,050 words) with a text search to check which expected items appear at all. Relevant counts: "adopt" 28, "workaround" 20, "measure" 8, "value" 6, "interface" 4, "training" 3, "outcome" 3, "trust" 2, "evidence" 2, "research" 1, "quality" 1, "data" 1, "cost" 1; "satisf", "survey", "study", "baseline", "benefit", "govern", "safety", "security", "privacy" and "feedback" each 0. A zero count is only a prompt to read the text again, because the article can cover an idea in other words.

## What the model says is present

Most DeLone and McLean dimensions are covered, in the article's own terms:

| Dimension | Where it appears |
|---|---|
| Use | The whole diagnosis: adoption "counts use". |
| Net benefits | "whether the work is done better, faster or more reliably, which is what the original investment was for", and the medium term tier of time, quality, errors and experience. |
| System quality | The interface and speed workarounds ("acceptable speed"). |
| Information quality | One phrase: "how good its data is". |
| Service quality | Only indirectly, as training time and a named accountable person for team workarounds. |
| User satisfaction | Only indirectly, as trust and "the experience of staff and customers". |

The article's separation of use from value matches the model's separation of use from net benefits. That supports the diagnosis that use is a weak stand-in for benefit, but E4 as summarised does not say adoption measures are the dominant practice, so it cannot confirm that part.

## Expected but absent items

| ID | Item expected | Why it would be expected | Strength of expectation | Status in the article |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | A source or sample for the claim that boards, executives, vendors and consultancies behave as described ("Boards mostly point AI at cost reduction", "vendors set their pricing based on seats and usage") | The diagnosis is empirical, and the opening paragraph carries the factual premise of the whole piece. | Strong | Absent. No source is cited. |
| A2 | Evidence behind the workaround examples | The article says "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation." A claim of research would normally name or describe it. | Strong | Absent. The research is not identified, and the count, setting and method are not given. The article does not say how common any workaround is. |
| A3 | Any case where high usage does track real value | A fair test of "use and effective work can move in opposite directions" needs the cases where they move together. | Moderate | Absent. Only the divergent case (ten attempts, then finishing by hand) is given. |
| A4 | Evidence that the proposed tiers work, or any organisation that has used them | The article recommends a replacement measure. A recommendation is normally accompanied by some trial or reasoned comparison. | Moderate | Absent. The tiers are justified only as established practice, and the closing paragraph says "none of these tiers is new". |
| A5 | The measurement problem for the proposed outcome measures | The article itself says value "does not show up quickly in financial results" and few can trace it to AI. The same attribution problem applies to the medium term tier. | Strong | Mostly absent. It names the comparison with "how it was done before", but not what happens when there is no earlier version. It says that for work that is removed there is no earlier version, yet the medium term tier still depends on a comparison. |
| A6 | How workarounds are to be found without the honesty problem it describes | Its leadership and team examples show people hiding or disguising use. An observation based method needs a reason to expect staff to be candid. | Moderate | Partly present. The leadership fix (a statement of how figures will be used) addresses candour, but the short term tier does not say how observation avoids the same distortion. |
| A7 | The cost of observing work and recording workarounds | The proposed short term measure is more labour intensive than counting logins, and the article says adoption is used because it "can be counted from the first week". | Moderate | Absent. |
| A8 | Workarounds that are beneficial or that fix a real fault in the tool | The article treats every workaround as showing "where the design failed". Some workarounds could instead reflect personal preference or an unsafe shortcut. | Moderate | Partly absent. The task example (staff changing records so a review does not trigger) is shown as a design failure with no mention that it could bypass a needed control. |
| A9 | Risk, compliance and safety dimensions of AI success | The user's brief is about AI measures, and an AI risk lens is a common part of organisational reporting. | Weak | Absent. Counts for governance, safety, security and privacy are all zero. The article may be deliberately limited to value and design. |
| A10 | User satisfaction and service quality as named measures | These are separate dimensions in E4. | Weak to moderate | Only indirect. The article is about tools and workflow design and need not use the model's vocabulary. |
| A11 | The feedback from net benefits to later use | E4 says net benefits feed back into use and satisfaction. This would temper the claim that use is unrelated to value, because use could be a reasonable lagging signal. | Weak | Absent. |
| A12 | Date, publisher or author context | The source line notes that date and publisher are not given. | Weak | Cannot be judged from the material. |

## What the absences say about the brief

On accuracy of the diagnosis, the missing items are sourcing items (A1, A2). The diagnosis that adoption counts use and not value is supported by the article's reasoning, and E4 supports separating use from net benefits. But the premise that organisations in practice measure this way, and the frequency of workarounds, rest on assertion.

On the validity of the point of view, the strongest absences are A2 and A5. The article asks the reader to accept workaround observations it does not describe, and it proposes outcome measures without confronting the attribution problem it raises in its first paragraph.

What the article leaves out that the model would expect is limited. Information quality, system quality, service quality and net benefits are reachable in the text, and satisfaction is implied. The absence of risk, governance and security (A9) and of explicit satisfaction (A10) is weak evidence of an omission, because the article does not claim to give a complete account of AI success.

## Conclusion

The absences count as limited evidence. They are strong only where the article makes an empirical claim and gives no basis for it (A1, A2) or where it raises a problem and does not apply it to its own proposal (A5). None of the absences indicates concealment. Several are consistent with a short opinion piece that is not meant to be a complete account. The honest reading is that the reasoning is coherent but the evidence for its premises is thin and not shown.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The technique assumes each item is expected for a stated reason. For A1, A2 and A5 the reason comes from the article's own claims. For A9 to A11 the reason comes only from E4 and from my judgement of what an AI measurement piece normally covers, so those are weaker.
- E4 was read as a summary only (abstract and descriptions in other papers), so I could not check how the model defines each dimension in detail.
- The term counts are literal text matches and do not capture paraphrase. I read the article in full to confirm each status.
- The technique cannot say whether the research claimed in A2 exists, only that the article does not show it.
- The fit test says absence is weak evidence when the author did not intend a complete account. This is a short opinion style piece of unknown date and publisher, so the weight of A3, A4 and A7 to A11 in particular is low.
- No external sources on how common adoption based measurement is were used, as the rules limit this to the material.

## Alternative explanations

- The article may be written as a position piece and not as a study. Read that way, the missing sources (A1, A2) are a genre choice, and its claims are offered as a design argument to be tested by the reader's own experience.
- The omission of risk, governance and satisfaction (A9, A10) may reflect a deliberate focus on design and workflow, which the author labels "WX", and not a gap in thinking.
- The missing counterexample (A3) and missing attribution problem (A5) could be a result of space (about 2,050 words) and not of one sided reasoning.
- The article's final paragraph says the tiers come from established practice, so the lack of a trial for them (A4) could be seen as intentional: the author is relying on prior evidence for those practices, which the article does not cite but which exists outside the material.

# Lens application: the article's claims sorted by the DeLone and McLean dimensions

## Material and conventions

The article has no item IDs, so items are referred to by the line number in /home/claude/sim_run/analysis_run/material/article.md (shown as L plus the number) and by IDs I assigned while listing (M, C, W and P). Counts below were produced by a script run over the table in this file.

## Step 1: items listed

Thirty-five items were listed: the measures the article says organisations use (M), the claims in its diagnosis (C), its five levels of workaround (W) and its four proposed measurement tiers (P). Long claims that bundle several ideas were split where the ideas fall in different categories (for example, L8 on what usage cannot show was split into C3 to C6).

## Step 2: lens chosen

The lens is the six dimensions of the updated DeLone and McLean model (E4): information quality, system quality, service quality, use, user satisfaction and net benefits. E4 states that use is separate from net benefits, that use and satisfaction influence net benefits, and that net benefits feed back into later use. I added a seventh row, "outside the lens", for claims that none of the six dimensions covers. Without it those claims would have been forced into the most common category, which is the failure this technique warns about.

## Step 3: category definitions

E4 names the dimensions but does not define them. The one-line definitions below are mine and are the standard reading of the names, so they are an assumption.

- Information quality: how accurate, complete and relevant the information or data the system holds or produces is.
- System quality: how well the system works as built, including fit to the task, integration, usability and speed.
- Service quality: the support around the system, such as training, help and accountable owners.
- Use: whether, how often and in what way people use the system.
- User satisfaction: people's response to the system, including trust and experience.
- Net benefits: the effect on work, customers, staff or the organisation, including cost and productivity.
- Outside the lens: claims about job design, incentives, analogy or the article's own reasoning.

## Steps 4 and 5: table of items by category

Each item has one primary category. A secondary category is given where the item fits two.

| Category | Items (ID, line, short description, secondary category) |
|---|---|
| Use (10) | M1 L5 count of people using an app or agent; M2 L5 frequency of use of AI features; M3 L5 tokens consumed; M4 L4 vendor pricing on seats and usage; C1 L6 use and effective work diverge (also net benefits); C2 L7 parallel running still counts as adopted; C10 L11 people do not literally adopt AI (also outside the lens); C11 L14 a person uses a tool with AI built in; C14 L20 tool used as designed or by workaround (also system quality); C15 L21 workaround does not appear as non-use |
| System quality (6) | C3 L8 usage cannot show fit to task or connection to other tools; W1 L23 interface workaround; W2 L24 task workaround; W3 L25 workflow workaround; C16 L31 each workaround shows which part of the design failed; P1 L43 short term measure, tools work as designed |
| Information quality (1) | C4 L8 usage cannot show data quality |
| Service quality (1) | W4 L26 team workaround, no time to train |
| User satisfaction (1) | C5 L8 usage cannot show whether people trust what the tool produces (also information quality) |
| Net benefits (10) | M5 L5 usage read as a stand-in for headcount (also use); M6 L4 boards aim at cost reduction and customer service; M7 L4 executives report productivity gains; C6 L8 usage cannot show work done better, faster or more reliably; C7 L9 value from removing work is invisible to adoption; C8 L9 example of documents updating automatically; C9 L9 example of a product built so an error cannot happen; P2 L44 medium term measure (also user satisfaction); P3 L45 longer term measure (also outside the lens); P4 L46 end state measure |
| Outside the lens (6) | C12 L15 a person learns a new job (also net benefits); C13 L17 web search analogy; W5 L27 leadership workaround (also use); C17 L32 failure is attributed to people; C18 L47 none of the tiers is new; C19 L41 adoption is itself a workaround |

Counts by primary category: use 10, system quality 6, information quality 1, service quality 1, user satisfaction 1, net benefits 10, outside the lens 6. Total 35. Nine items have a secondary category.

Two subsets give a sharper picture:

| Subset | Use | System quality | Information quality | Service quality | User satisfaction | Net benefits |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Measures the article says organisations use or report (M1 to M7) | 4 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 3 |
| Measures the article proposes instead (P1 to P4) | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 3 |

(P2 and P3 each have a secondary category, not counted here. Of the four proposed tiers, three are net benefits and one is system quality.)

## Step 6: reading the spread

**Where claims cluster.** Use and net benefits hold 20 of the 35 items. This matches the article's own framing, which is a contrast between counting use and measuring the benefit of the work. System quality is the third cluster (6 items), and it is where almost all of the workaround material sits (W1 to W3, C16, P1).

**Thin categories.** Information quality has one item (C4), service quality has one (W4) and user satisfaction has one (C5). None of the three has a measure attached. The article names data quality (L8) and trust (L8) as things usage cannot show, and names training (L26, L37) as a fix, but it proposes no way to measure any of them. Its proposed tiers contain no item whose primary category is information quality, service quality or user satisfaction.

**Claims without evidence of any kind.** No item in the table is supported in the article by data. The only statement about evidence is L29: "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation." No study, count, organisation or source is named. The claims that organisations report adoption (L4), that vendors price on seats and usage (L4) and that "Adoption seems to have gone mainstream" (L4) are also stated without support. The material cannot show whether the diagnosis describes common practice.

**What the sort says about the diagnosis.** The core claim, that use is not the same as net benefits, is consistent with E4, where use is a separate dimension that influences net benefits rather than standing in for it. The article is accurate in that narrow sense. The sort also shows that the article's "adoption" is only the use dimension. The other dimensions that the model treats as routine measures (user satisfaction, information quality, service quality) are not described as measured or as missing from existing programs. The article does not say whether organisations also collect them. The claim that adoption measures "cannot see workarounds" is argued by definition (L21) and by illustrations (L23 to L27), not by any count of what programs actually measure.

**What the sort says about the point of view.** The proposed replacement is weighted to net benefits (3 of 4 tiers) and system quality (1 of 4). The article's argument for abandoning use as a headline measure is reasoned, but two steps are not supported in the text. One is the step from "workaround present" to "design failed" (L31): the article states this as a general rule and does not consider workarounds that arise from other causes. L26 itself lists lack of training time, which is a service quality cause, and L27 lists an incentive cause. The other step is the claim at L17 that AI will become a component of everything, offered through the web search analogy only. The medium and longer tiers (L44, L45) depend on before and after comparison, which the article itself says is impossible for work that is removed (L9), so the tiers do not cover the category of value the article calls the largest gap. The article's last paragraph (L47) concedes the tiers are not new, which weakens the framing of the proposal as a workaround of its own.

## Borderline assignments

- C1 (L6) is about the relation between use and benefit. It is placed in use because it describes what use figures show, with net benefits as secondary.
- C5 (L8): trust in output could be read as information quality or user satisfaction. It is placed in user satisfaction. If it moved to information quality, that category would have two items and user satisfaction none.
- W4 (L26) is placed in service quality because the stated cause is training time. The team's behaviour is also a form of use, so a different rater could place it there.
- W5 (L27) and C12 (L15) are placed outside the lens. A rater who stretched use to cover the manager's management of recorded usage would move W5 to use, raising use to 11.
- M5 (L5) is placed in net benefits because it concerns the financial meaning given to usage. It could equally be use.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The technique assumed written category definitions. E4 supplies only the dimension names, so the definitions are mine and a different reader could define them differently.
- The sort depends on how I split the article into items. Splitting L8 into four items raised the counts for information quality, user satisfaction and system quality. Left as one item it would sit in one category and the thin categories would look thinner still.
- The article is one text with no stated date or publisher, and the page could not be fetched (L1). The material says nothing about what organisations actually measure.
- The technique shows which kinds of claim are present. It does not test whether any claim is true, and it cannot tell whether the missing categories are missing from the article or from the organisations it describes.
- I added a seventh category, which is outside the technique's usual form. Six items needed it.
- Counts were produced by a script over my own table, so they reflect my assignments and are not independent ratings. No second rater was available to test agreement, so the fit test (that two raters assign the same way) was not run.

## Alternative explanations

- The thin information quality, service quality and user satisfaction rows may reflect the article's purpose rather than a gap in its thinking. It is a short argument against one measure (use), so it would be expected to concentrate on use and net benefits. The absence of other dimensions could be scope, not omission.
- The system quality cluster may come from the article's own organising device (five levels of workaround) rather than from where the author's evidence lies. The structure produces six items there by construction.
- The absence of cited evidence may mean the article is an opinion piece written from practice, where the observations at L29 are the author's own. The material cannot distinguish an unreported study from an unsupported assertion.
- The weight on use and net benefits may be a feature of the lens. E4 gives use and net benefits their own dimensions, so an argument about adoption versus value falls into those two rows almost automatically.

# Definitional analysis of the key terms in the adoption and workaround article

## Scope

The brief asks whether the article accurately diagnoses a phenomenon (organisations measure AI transformation by adoption, and adoption measures miss workarounds and value) and whether its point of view is valid. Several terms in that question carry more than one meaning, in the question and in the article. This result replaces each with a working definition and tests it against borderline cases taken from the article's own examples. The material is one article, so no other source is used. The article has no numbered items, so passages are identified by section heading.

The technique needs at least two usages of each term. The article supplies two or more for every term below. The one exception is "evidence", where the article gives only one explicit statement, and this is noted in that entry.

## Glossary

### 1. Adoption

**Usages in the article**

- A counted quantity. Section "Adoption" opening paragraphs: adoption "counts use: how many people use an app or agent, how often they use its AI features, and how many tokens they consume".
- A stand-in for headcount reduction. "High usage suggests the same work could be done by fewer people".
- A normative state of effective work. Section "People use a tool as designed or work around it": "If adoption means anything at work, it means the tool works well enough, as designed, for people to get the job done with it."
- A claim about what people do. "AI adoption assumes that people actually "adopt AI". Taken literally, they do not."
- A coping device. "adoption is itself a workaround".

**Working definitions (the term needs two, kept apart)**

- Adoption (measured): the recorded use of a tool or agent that contains AI, such as active licences, session counts, feature calls or tokens consumed, over a period. This is what the article attacks as a measure.
- Adoption (effective): people completing their work with the tool in the way it was designed, with the tool being good enough for that. This is the article's own standard in the third usage above.

**Why two definitions are needed.** The article's central claim is that measured adoption misses workarounds. Under the definition of effective adoption, a workaround is by definition the opposite of adoption, so the claim that adoption measures fail to see workarounds is partly true by definition. What is empirically open is how often measured adoption and effective adoption diverge, and the article gives no figure for that.

**Borderline cases**

| Case (from the article) | Measured adoption | Effective adoption |
|---|---|---|
| A person needing ten attempts, then finishing by hand | High (more tokens) | No |
| A team running old and new process in parallel | Full | No |
| A person using a tool with AI built in, unaware of which parts use AI | Counted if feature calls are logged, otherwise unclear | Yes, if used as designed, but the article says this is "not adopting AI" |
| A person who "learns a new job" reviewing agent exceptions | Counted only as use of the review tool | Unclear, because the article says usage figures cannot answer whether the job is well designed |
| A person using a personal tool because the approved tool is slow | Low for the approved tool | No for the approved tool, but possibly yes for AI generally |

**Where answers differ by definition:** the parallel-running team, the ten-attempt user and the personal-tool user. The first two are adopters under one definition and not under the other. The third is a non-adopter of the approved tool and a possible adopter of AI, so the answer depends on whether the unit is the tool or the technology.

### 2. AI transformation

**Usages in the article**

- Title: "a workaround for measuring AI transformation", which treats it as a programme with progress to be measured.
- Section "What an AI program should measure and do instead": an "end state", described as "the future it set out to reach", with redesigned work and "work that is no longer needed".
- Opening paragraph: enterprises "getting value from the AI-based solutions they deploy", which treats it as deployment of solutions.

**Working definition:** a programme of deliberate change to how work is done or what is delivered, in which AI is part of the means, judged by changes in work outcomes and not by the presence of AI.

**Why this definition.** The article's own position (AI becoming "a component of everything") implies that transformation cannot be defined as "increase in AI use". The definition therefore excludes use as a criterion and includes redesign of work.

**Borderline cases**

- Rolling out an email assistant to all staff with no change to any process. Deployment, but not transformation under this definition.
- The article's examples of work removed (documents that update automatically; a product built so an error cannot happen). Transformation under this definition, though the article says nothing in them "is being used more than it was before".
- A speed-up of an existing step. The article treats this as measurable value. Whether it is transformation or only improvement depends on whether the work's structure changed.

**Where answers differ by definition:** the email assistant and the speed-up. A deployment-based definition counts both. The definition above counts neither, and this changes whether the article's phenomenon (measuring transformation by adoption) is a measurement error or a category error about what is being measured.

### 3. Workaround

**Usages in the article**

- "they find a workaround that gets the job done" (as the alternative to using a tool as designed).
- Five levels, each with examples: interface, task, workflow, team, leadership.
- "adoption is itself a workaround", where the word is applied to a measurement practice.

**Working definition:** an action by a person that achieves a work outcome by a route other than the one the tool or process was designed for, because the designed route did not let them achieve it (or did not seem to). The article's causal clause ("because they are responsible for getting the work done and the tool as designed did not let them do it") is part of the definition it uses, so the working definition keeps it.

**Test against the article's own examples.** Not every example meets the definition.

| Example | Meets the definition? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Interface: other applications kept open beside the tool | Yes | Designed route insufficient, person compensates |
| Interface: personal tool used instead of the slow approved tool | Yes, but also a policy breach | The route is non-designed, and it moves AI use outside the measured tool |
| Task: staff change records so the agent skips the review | Borderline | It achieves the outcome by a non-designed route, but it removes a control, and the article does not say the review was needed or not |
| Workflow: rebuilding lost context from other tools | Yes | Clear compensation for a design gap |
| Team: opening the tool daily to record usage, then working the old way | Borderline | The workaround is of the measure and the training requirement, not of the tool's function |
| Leadership: keeping usage high enough to comply but low enough not to imply headcount cuts | Borderline | This manages the measure and its consequences. It does not route work around a tool |

**Where answers differ by definition:** the last three rows. If a workaround must achieve the work by another route, the team and leadership examples are gaming of a measure and fall outside the term. If a workaround is any behaviour that departs from designed use for a reason connected to the design or programme, they fall inside. This matters for the claim that "each workaround shows where the design failed": for the team and leadership cases, the failure shown is of the measurement and incentive arrangements, and not of tool design. The article's fix for those levels (time for training, honest reporting) is consistent with this, but its heading "Each workaround shows where the design failed" is wider than what these two examples support.

**A second borderline.** The article says a person "does one of two things": uses the tool as designed or finds a workaround. Partial use, mixed use and abandonment fit neither. Abandonment would appear in usage figures as low use, which is the case adoption measures do see. The two-way division therefore narrows the set of cases to those that favour the article's argument.

### 4. Value (and "value that adoption cannot see")

**Usages in the article**

- Value as board and executive outcomes: "cost reduction and customer service" and "productivity gains".
- Value as measurable improvement: "the same work now takes less time and can be compared with last year's figures".
- Value as work removed: "They remove the need for it."
- Value as the purpose of investment: whether work "is done better, faster or more reliably, which is what the original investment was for".

**Working definition:** a change in an outcome the organisation or its customers care about (cost, time, quality, error rate, experience), measured against a stated earlier state or counterfactual.

**Why a counterfactual is part of the definition.** The article says of removed work that "there is no earlier version of the work to compare it with". Under a comparison-based definition, removed work has value that cannot be measured by comparison, which is the article's point. Under a definition without a baseline, the value can be stated as a saved cost.

**Borderline cases**

- Removal of requests and follow-up calls (the document example). Real value, no baseline in the work itself, though a baseline exists in the earlier volume of requests, which the article does not mention.
- The error that "cannot happen". The checking team's earlier workload is a possible baseline.
- Workarounds found and removed, offered as a short-term measure. Whether this is value or only a process indicator depends on the definition, since it measures the removal of friction and not a work outcome.

**Where answers differ by definition:** the first two cases. The article says adoption "has no way to record this value". That is true of usage counts. It does not follow that the value cannot be measured at all, and the article's own medium-term tier tracks "time, quality, errors" against "how it was done before", which would apply to these cases. The article does not reconcile this with its statement that no earlier version exists.

### 5. Measure (and "adoption measure")

**Usages in the article**

- Usage counts reported as progress ("AI programs report adoption instead").
- The proposed tiers, which include observation and conversation ("Observe the work as it is done, ask people what they do").
- "Leadership workarounds need measures based on the outcomes of the work rather than on usage".

**Working definition:** a repeatable procedure that yields a comparable record of some property of the work or the tool, which can be reported to a programme over time. This includes qualitative records if the procedure is repeatable.

**Borderline cases**

- A count of "workarounds found and removed". It is countable, but its meaning depends on how thoroughly workarounds are looked for.
- Observation and interviews. Repeatable if structured, otherwise not.
- Token consumption. Countable, but the article uses it as a bad measure of effective work, while it also has a legitimate role in cost.

**Where answers differ by definition:** observation and interviews. If a measure must be numeric and comparable, the article's short-term tier is not a measure and the alternative it proposes to adoption is weaker than presented. If qualitative records count, the tier is a measure but is subject to the same question of how many are found, which is the weakness the article attributes to adoption counts.

### 6. Evidence (as in "supported by its own evidence")

**Usages in the article**

- "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation." This is the only statement about evidence for the five workaround levels.
- Statements about what boards, executives, vendors and consultancies do, given without any source.

The article gives one explicit evidence statement and one implicit pattern (unsourced claims of fact). The minimum of two usages is met only loosely.

**Working definition (for this analysis):** material in the article that a reader could check, meaning a named study, dataset, count or observation with an identifiable source, or an argument whose premises are stated and whose conclusion follows from them.

**Borderline cases**

- The workaround examples. The article says they are from research, but names no study, sample or setting. A reader cannot check them. They are usable as illustrations of a mechanism, not as evidence of frequency.
- The web search analogy. It is a historical example offered in support of the claim that AI will become an ordinary component. It is a single case.
- The statement that "none of these tiers is new". An argument from established practice, with no examples named.

**Where answers differ by definition:** the workaround examples. If evidence includes plausible illustrations of a mechanism, the article's claim that workarounds exist at every level is supported. If evidence requires a checkable source, the claim of frequency is unsupported, and the article's claim about the phenomenon (that organisations measure transformation by adoption) is also unsupported beyond its stated assertion, since no organisation, survey or example is cited for it.

## What the definitions show about the brief's question

1. The phenomenon, as defined above, has two parts with different support. That organisations report adoption is asserted in the first paragraph with no source. That adoption counts cannot distinguish designed use from workaround is supported by the logic of the definition of measured adoption (a count of use does not record how the use happened) and does not need empirical evidence.
2. The claim that adoption measures "miss workarounds" is largely true by definition once effective adoption is defined as the absence of workarounds. The article does not state which definition it is using at each point. This is the main definitional weakness.
3. The claim that adoption measures miss value is true for removed work only if "value" requires a baseline within the work itself. The article's own medium-term tier implies a baseline can be built, which is in tension with its statement about removed work.
4. The workaround category is wider than the article's heading suggests. Two of five levels (team and leadership) are behaviours aimed at the measure, so they show a failure of measurement and incentives and not of tool design.
5. The two-way division of behaviour (designed use or workaround) leaves out abandonment, partial use and legitimate use of AI outside the approved tool, and these are cases that usage counts would partly capture.
6. What the article leaves out, as shown by the borderline cases: any figure for how often adoption counts and effective use diverge; any case where high adoption does reflect effective use; any organisation that does measure by outcome already; and how the proposed tiers avoid the same problem of being reported as a number without meaning.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The technique assumed that the article's terms can be given stable definitions from the article's own usages. Where the article uses one term in several senses (adoption, workaround), the result keeps both senses and does not choose between them for the author.
- The working definitions are mine and are tested only against the article's examples. Two analysts might draw the lines differently, particularly for "workaround" and "evidence".
- The technique could not assess whether the phenomenon is real. It clarifies what would count as the phenomenon. The article names no organisation, survey or study, and the material holds nothing to check the claims about boards, executives or vendors.
- The technique did not count anything in the text. No code was used, because the technique does not call for counting or text comparison.
- Quotations were selected from the article as supplied. The material states that the page could not be fetched and the text was supplied by the user, so it may differ from the published version. The date and publisher are not given.
- The term "point of view valid" was not given its own glossary entry, because its content is covered by the entries for adoption, workaround, value, measure and evidence.

## Alternative explanations

- The article may mean "adoption" in one consistent sense, the narrow counted sense, and use the normative sentence ("If adoption means anything at work...") only as a rhetorical contrast. On that reading there is no equivocation, and the claim that counts miss workarounds is a straightforward point about what counts record. The definitional tension I found would then be a matter of presentation, not of reasoning.
- The wider workaround category may be intended. The article may treat gaming of a measure as a workaround of the programme, so that team and leadership examples belong in the term by design. On that reading the heading "Each workaround shows where the design failed" refers to the design of the programme and its incentives, not only of the tools, and the mismatch I found is a matter of wording.
- The apparent conflict between "no earlier version" and the medium-term comparison with "how it was done before" may be a difference of scale. The first refers to a single removed task, the second to the whole piece of work the programme changes. On that reading the two statements are consistent.
- The absence of cited evidence may reflect the form (a short opinion article on a blog platform) and not a weakness in the underlying research the article says it draws on.
