# Competing hypotheses on the article's diagnosis and point of view

This result applies analysis of competing hypotheses (ACH) to the brief: is the article's diagnosis accurate and is its point of view valid. The article has no item IDs, so article items are labelled A1 to A7 (claims and arguments) and O1 and O2 (omissions). E1 (METR) and E2 (Microsoft and LinkedIn vendor survey) keep their evidence IDs. E2 shows what the vendor reports, not what is true of the world, and E1 does not independently confirm it, so E2 rows are not treated as confirmation.

## Hypotheses

- H1: The diagnosis is accurate and the article's claims are supported by its own evidence.
- H2: The diagnosis is plausible and partly supported, but the article asserts more than it shows (its evidence is illustrative and its causal and general claims are unsourced).
- H3: The phenomenon is real but the article places the problem wrongly. The main measurement problem is that usage overstates effect, and workarounds are secondary.
- H4: The premise is weak or not general: organisations already measure outcomes as well, so the article argues against a narrower practice than it describes.

Ratings: C is consistent, I is inconsistent, N is neutral or not applicable. Inconsistencies carry the weight, because consistent evidence rarely rules a hypothesis out.

## Matrix

| ID | Evidence item | H1 | H2 | H3 | H4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Opening premise that boards point AI at cost reduction and customer service, that few organisations can trace value to AI, and that AI programs therefore report adoption. No source or count is given. | I | C | C | C |
| A2 | The statement "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation." It comes after the five workaround levels and cites no study, participants or counts. | I | C | C | C |
| A3 | Logic of the measurement gaps: more tokens can mean less effective work, parallel running still counts as adopted, and removed work has no earlier version to compare with. | C | C | C | N |
| A4 | Analogies (ecommerce, cloud, web search) used to argue that people do not adopt AI but use tools or learn jobs. | C | C | C | N |
| A5 | Five level taxonomy of workarounds (interface, task, workflow, team, leadership), each described with an example and no frequency. | C | C | N | N |
| A6 | Causal chain: "A program measured by adoption rates cannot see workarounds, so when the work does not improve it has no evidence about the design and looks for the cause in people instead." Stated as fact, not shown. | I | C | C | C |
| A7 | Concession that "none of these tiers is new" and that adoption is itself a workaround for lack of a clearer picture. | C | C | C | C |
| O1 | Omission: no data on how many organisations measure by adoption, or how many already measure outcomes as well. | I | C | C | C |
| O2 | Omission: no evidence that finding and removing workarounds improves value, and no cost or measurability discussion of the proposed tiers. | I | C | C | N |
| E1a | E1: developers forecast AI would cut time by 24%, believed after the tasks it had cut time by 20%, yet tasks took 19% longer with AI. Use and belief diverged from measured work (software development, 16 developers). | C | C | C | N |
| E1b | E1: the same divergence shows that self-report can be wrong, which bears on the article's short term step of asking people what they do (the article also says to observe the work). | N | C | C | N |
| E2a | E2 (vendor): 78% of AI users bring their own AI tools to work. Matches the interface example of a personal tool replacing the approved one. | C | C | N | N |
| E2b | E2 (vendor): 79% of leaders agree AI adoption is critical to stay competitive. Shows adoption is a leadership priority, not how it is measured. | C | C | C | I |
| E2c | E2 (vendor): 39% of users have received company AI training and 60% of leaders say the company lacks a vision and plan. Matches the team level and end state concerns. | C | C | C | N |
| E2d | E2 (vendor, via Axios): 53% of AI users worry that revealing AI use signals they are replaceable. Matches concealment, but it points to usage figures understating use, not overstating it. | C | C | I | N |
| | Count of I | 5 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| | Count of C | 9 | 15 | 12 | 5 |
| | Count of N | 1 | 0 | 2 | 9 |

There are 15 evidence items. Counts were computed by code from the ratings above.

## Evidence that discriminates

Items where at least one hypothesis is rated inconsistent and the ratings differ: A1, A2, A6, O1, O2, E2b, E2d.

- A1, A2, A6, O1 and O2 are inconsistent with H1 only. The article's central premise, its claim of observational research and its causal chain are stated without evidence, and it gives no data on how widespread adoption based measurement is. These items separate H1 from H2 and H3.
- E2d is inconsistent with H3 only. A vendor reported worry about revealing AI use suggests usage figures can understate use, which counts against the view that usage mainly overstates effect. The source is a vendor survey, so this is weak.
- E2b is inconsistent with H4 only. Leaders calling adoption critical fits an adoption focus, but it does not show adoption is how progress is measured, so it is a weak discriminator.

Items that do not discriminate: A3, A4, A5, A7, E1a, E1b, E2a, E2c. These are rated consistent or neutral everywhere. The internal logic (A3), the analogies (A4), the workaround taxonomy (A5), the concession in A7, and the E1 and E2 figures that match the article's examples all fit every hypothesis, so they should not move the conclusion. In particular E1a shows that use and effect can diverge, but it is software development only, and it is not about adoption metrics or workarounds.

## Result

H2 has the fewest inconsistencies (0), followed by H3 (1) and H4 (1), which tie. H1 has the most (5). On this material the article's diagnosis reads as plausible and its reasoning as internally sound, but its point of view is not supported by its own evidence to the standard its tone implies. The strongest points against it are the unsourced premise, the uncited claim of observational research, and the unshown causal chain from adoption figures to blaming people.

What the article assumes: that adoption reporting is the dominant practice, that workarounds are common enough to matter, and that fixing them raises value. What it leaves out: any count of organisations, any outcome from the proposed measures, and any evidence on the cost of observing work. It does state its own limit honestly in one place, by conceding that none of its tiers is new.

H2 beats H4 narrowly, and the margin depends on a single item (E2b) from a vendor source, so the ordering of H2, H3 and H4 is not firm. The separation of H1 from the others is firmer, because it rests on five article internal items.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The hypothesis list is mine and may be incomplete. H3 and H4 are the rivals I judged most plausible from the brief.
- Ratings are judgements about fit, not measurements. Another rater could move some C and N cells.
- Equal weight was given to every item, though items differ in strength. E2 items come from a vendor survey read only as a summary, and E1 was read only as a summary.
- The article could not be checked against any external population of organisations, so the premise that adoption is the dominant measure was tested only against what the article says and against E2b.
- H2 is rated consistent on every item, which makes it the hardest to refute and the broadest hypothesis. Its low count partly reflects that breadth. H4 is rated neutral on 9 items, so the material tells us little about it.
- Some inconsistencies for H1 are of one kind (missing evidence), so they are not five independent strikes.

## Alternative explanations

- The article may be a practitioner's argument from design experience, not a study. On that reading the missing sources are a genre choice, and H1 should be judged on plausibility and usefulness, not on citation.
- The inconsistencies for H1 may reflect the evidence supplied to this analysis (a summary of one trial and one vendor report) more than the article's real support. A fuller evidence base could shift the ratings.
- The ordering of H2 ahead of H4 may come from my choice of hypotheses. If H4 were framed as a claim about specific industries, it might rank differently.
results.TC1-16:
# Disconfirmation search on the favoured reading of the adoption article

## Claim under test

The seven earlier results (FQ-03, TC1-19, TC1-21, CM1-01, CM1-14, DM-07, TC1-13) jointly favour this reading, which I restate as three parts so each can be tested.

- Part A (narrow diagnosis). A usage count (users, frequency, tokens) cannot tell designed use from a workaround, and cannot record value that comes from removing work. This follows from what a usage count records.
- Part B (empirical premises). The article asserts, and does not show, that organisations mostly report adoption as progress, that workarounds are common, and that the five-level examples are real observations.
- Part C (point of view). The article overreaches when it says every workaround shows a design failure, when it treats adoption as a literal error, and when it offers its tiers as a remedy without evidence that they work.

The brief needs a description only, and the stakes are exploratory, so the aim is to record what would contradict the reading and whether it turned up, not to prove the reading.

## What would refute the claim (written before searching)

The following list was fixed before I searched the article or the evidence files.

| ID | Evidence that would refute the claim | Part tested |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | The article names a study, sample, count or organisation for its workaround examples or for its statements about boards, vendors and consultancies | B |
| R2 | The article, E1 or E2 shows high usage going together with good outcomes, or shows organisations already measuring outcomes | A and B |
| R3 | Usage data would in fact reveal the article's workarounds (for example as non-use or low use), so the claim that they look like active use fails | A |
| R4 | The article, or the other findings, show that value from removed work can be measured by a before and after comparison | A |
| R5 | The article supplies a ground or example showing that team and leadership workarounds are design failures of the tool, or that its two-case split of behaviour is complete | C |
| R6 | One of the seven findings contradicts the joint reading, or a finding rests on a misquotation of the article | All |
| R7 | The evidence files (E1 to E3) contradict the article's mechanism, or show that its proposed measures would work | B and C |
| R8 | The article supports its claim that AI will become a component of everything, or that programs blame people when design is the cause | C |

## Search and results by item

The search was run over the article text (read in full), the seven findings (read in full) and E1 to E3. External sources were not used, because the technique needs none and the rules limit the work to the material. Text searches were literal matches, so a zero count prompted a second read and not a conclusion.

### R1: a source for the workaround examples or the premises

- Search used: literal searches of the article for "survey", "study", "%", "research", "evidence" and "already", then a full read of the opening paragraph and the workaround section.
- Result: not found. "survey", "study", "%" and "already" each return zero lines. "research" returns one line: "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation." It names no study, setting, sample or date. "evidence" appears twice, once about what people explain failure by and once in "A program still needs early evidence", and neither supplies a source. Every earlier finding that checked this (TC1-19, TC1-21, CM1-14, DM-07) reached the same result independently.
- Bearing: this item is the main support for Part B and was not refuted.

### R2: high usage with good outcomes, or outcomes already measured

- Search used: searches of the article for "outcome", "correlat" and "already", then a read of E1 and E2 for any result linking usage to results.
- Result: not found in the article. The word "outcome" appears three times, only in the proposed fixes. No passage describes a programme that measures outcomes today, or a case of usage and results moving together. E1 does not help in either direction: it records that developers believed AI had cut their time by 20% while tasks took 19% longer, so belief and result diverged in one small trial, which is one case and is not about usage counts. E2 reports that 75% of knowledge workers use AI and that 79% of leaders agree adoption is critical, which shows a priority on adoption and says nothing about how it is measured or whether it tracks results.
- Bearing: nothing refutes the claim. The absence of a counterexample is also a gap in the article (it never tests its own claim against cases where usage did match value), as CM1-14 (A3) and FQ-03 noted. I do not read this as confirmation of the article, only as a failure to find a refuter in the material.

### R3: usage data would reveal the workarounds

- Search used: a re-read of the five workaround levels against the sentence "A workaround does not show up as non-use", then a check of E2.
- Result: found in part. The article's own interface example says "the approved tool is slow, so people use a personal one instead". That behaviour would show as low use of the approved tool, which is what a usage count does detect. E2 reports that 78% of AI users bring their own AI tools to work, and that fits this example. The statement "A workaround does not show up as non-use" is therefore true for some workarounds (parallel running, token use then finishing by hand, daily token opening) and false for others (substitution by a personal tool, abandonment). FQ-03 noted this for personal tools and abandonment, and TC1-21 (entry 7) noted that the two-way split leaves out non-use. The article's own claim is broader than its examples support.
- Bearing: this partly refutes Part A as I stated it, because the narrow diagnosis holds only for workarounds that keep the tool open. It does not refute the core logic, because the parallel-running and ten-attempt cases still follow from how counts work. The favoured reading should say "some workarounds", not "workarounds".

### R4: removed-work value can be measured by comparison

- Search used: a read of the article's "largest gap" paragraph and the medium-term tier, then a check of FQ-03, TC1-19 and TC1-21 for the same point.
- Result: found in part. The article says removed work has "no earlier version of the work to compare it with", yet its medium-term tier says to track "time, quality, errors, and the experience of staff and customers for each piece of work the program changes, compared with how it was done before". FQ-03 observed that earlier request volumes and the checking team's workload could serve as a baseline. The article also says that for sped-up steps "the same work now takes less time and can be compared with last year's figures". So the article's remedy implies that some comparison is possible, which weakens the claim that this value is invisible, though only to usage counts, which is what the article actually says ("An adoption measure has no way to record this value"). The claim about usage counts is untouched.
- Bearing: the claim that this value cannot be recorded by adoption measures survives. The stronger reading that such value is unmeasurable by any method is contradicted by the article's own remedy. Three findings (FQ-03, TC1-19, TC1-21) already flag the tension.

### R5: support for the design-failure claim or the two-case split

- Search used: a read of the team and leadership examples and their stated fixes, and of the passage "falls into two cases".
- Result: not found. The team example (nobody had time for training) and the leadership example (a manager manages recorded usage) are failures of workload and incentives. Their stated fixes are "time to learn the new way of working" and "a clear statement of how adoption figures will and will not be used", which are not changes to the tool. The two-case split is asserted as complete with no argument. TC1-19 and TC1-21 reached the same result.
- Bearing: Part C was not refuted. A defence exists (design in a wide sense that includes work organisation), but it is the article's WX idea and the article does not state it in this text.

### R6: a finding that contradicts the joint reading, or misquotes the article

- Search used: a comparison of the seven findings' conclusions against each other, and a check of quoted passages against the article for the ones I relied on.
- Result: not found as a contradiction, with two points of difference in weight.
  - TC1-13 favours H2 (plausible but over-asserted) over H3 and H4 by a narrow margin that rests on one vendor item (E2b), and TC1-13 says so. The ordering of H2, H3 and H4 is therefore not firm. TC1-13's separation of H1 (the article is fully supported) from the others is firmer.
  - TC1-21 entry 11 raises a possible inconsistency between "few organisations can trace either back to AI specifically" and "the gain can be measured" for sped-up steps. It treats the two as possibly reconcilable (measuring a gain differs from attributing it to AI), and I agree, so this does not contradict the joint reading.
  - The quotations I checked match the article. I did not re-check every quotation in every finding.
- Bearing: the findings agree on the shape of the conclusion. They are not independent in the strong sense, because they all read one article and four of them (TC1-19, TC1-21, CM1-14, DM-07) share the same missing-source observation, which counts as one observation made several times and not as several confirmations.

### R7: the evidence files contradict the mechanism or show the proposals work

- Search used: a read of E1, E2 and E3 for any result bearing on workarounds, concealment, attribution, or the effect of outcome measures.
- Result: found in part, in three places, none of which refutes the diagnosis.
  - E1 shows that after the tasks the developers still believed AI had cut time by 20%, when it had increased time by 19%. This weakens the article's short-term tier, which relies partly on asking people what they do ("ask people what they do when a tool does not give them what they need"), because self-report was wrong in this trial. The tier also says to observe the work, and E1 does not test observation. E1 covers 16 developers in one task type with early-2025 tools.
  - E2's 53% worry about revealing AI use fits concealment, but concealment of use would make usage counts understate use, not overstate effect. It also bears on the proposed tier: if people hide use for fear of being replaceable, observation and interviews face the same distortion the article attributes to usage figures. E2 is a vendor survey whose method I did not read, and it records worry, not behaviour.
  - E3 says that earlier measures of IT productivity were "almost impossible to assess" and the evidence was inconclusive, and that new data later gave positive results. That fits the idea that measures can be part of the problem. It gives no evidence on workarounds, and it shows that established methods did not settle the matter for years, which weakens the article's closing line that "we've done this before with methods that still work" (CM1-01, element 12).
- Bearing: no item contradicts Part A. E1 and E2 give weak reasons to doubt the remedy (Part C), which the earlier findings already identified. None shows that the proposed tiers would work or fail.

### R8: support for the prediction about AI as a component, or for the people-blaming claim

- Search used: a read of the web search passage and of "When an adoption does not work out".
- Result: not found. The prediction rests on one analogy (web search). The claim about common explanations ("staff are resisting, that leaders are not engaged enough, or that the organisation did not follow the program") has no source or case. The article does not name a programme that blamed people when design was at fault.
- Bearing: Part C stands.

## Summary table

| ID | Refuting evidence | Found or not found | Effect on the claim |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Source for examples or premises | Not found | Part B stands |
| R2 | High usage with good outcomes, or outcomes already measured | Not found | No refutation, and the article never tests the case |
| R3 | Usage data would reveal the workarounds | Found in part (personal tool, abandonment) | Part A needs "some workarounds" |
| R4 | Removed-work value is measurable by comparison | Found in part (the article's own medium-term tier) | Survives for usage counts, fails for "unmeasurable" |
| R5 | Support for design-failure claim or two-case split | Not found | Part C stands |
| R6 | A contradicting finding or misquotation | Not found | The H2 to H4 ordering is not firm |
| R7 | Evidence files contradict the mechanism or support the remedy | Found in part (E1, E2, E3), none against Part A | Slight extra doubt on the remedy |
| R8 | Support for the prediction or the people-blaming claim | Not found | Part C stands |

## What the findings mean for the claim

The favoured reading survived the search with one correction and two caveats.

- Correction. Part A should be narrowed. Usage counts hide workarounds that keep the tool open (parallel running, repeated attempts followed by manual finishing, daily token opening). They do not hide a workaround that replaces the tool or an abandoned tool, which appear as low use. The article's sentence "A workaround does not show up as non-use" is wider than its own examples.
- Caveat on Part A and the remedy. The claim that value from removed work is invisible holds for usage counts. It does not hold for measurement in general, as the article's own medium-term tier shows.
- Caveat on independence. The agreement among the seven findings is weaker than seven separate confirmations, because the findings share one article and one evidence set, and the missing-source point recurs in four of them.

Parts B and C were not refuted. Nothing in the article or the three evidence files I read supplies a source for the premises, a counterexample, or support for the design-failure claim. That is a statement about what this search found in a small body of material. It does not show that such evidence does not exist elsewhere, and it does not show that the article is right.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The refuter list is mine and may be incomplete. I wrote it before searching, but it reflects what I judged an informed critic would raise. A different list, for example one that asks whether the article's examples match published studies of enterprise workarounds, would need external material, which the rules excluded.
- The search covers a small body of text: one article of roughly 2,000 words, seven findings and three evidence summaries. A finding of "not found" here is weak evidence about the world. This is the failure the technique warns about, and I have not treated it as confirmation.
- E1, E2 and E3 were read only as search summaries, and E2 is a vendor survey whose method was not read. E4 was not read, because the instruction named E1 to E3.
- Text searches were literal and would miss paraphrase. I read the relevant passages in full after each search, but a refuting phrase in other words could still have been missed.
- The article text was supplied because the page could not be fetched, and it gives no date or publisher. It may differ from the published version.
- I did not re-run the earlier techniques. Where I rely on a finding, I rely on its stated reading of the article and checked its quotations selectively.

## Alternative explanations

- The search may have found little because the article is a practitioner's position piece that does not set out to prove prevalence. On that reading, the missing sources reflect genre, and the right test is plausibility and usefulness, which the narrow diagnosis passes.
- The partial refutations (R3, R4) may reflect loose wording and not faulty reasoning. "A workaround does not show up as non-use" may be meant for the cases where the person keeps using the tool, and "no earlier version" may refer to a single removed task and not to a whole programme. If so, the correction to Part A is a matter of phrasing.
- The agreement among the earlier findings may be partly produced by the shared evidence set and shared framing. A reader starting from a different lens, for example organisational incentives, might weigh the team and leadership examples as the article's strongest material and the tool-design claim as the weakest, which would change the emphasis but not the facts found here.
- The lack of any counterexample (R2) could mean such cases are rare, or only that the article and the evidence summaries were not built to include them. The material cannot separate these.

- Consistency is not correctness. All seven files could share a mistaken premise, for example about what counts as a workaround, without any conflict showing here.

- The conflicts in findings 1, 4 and 5 may come from each technique having a different purpose. A glossary, a Toulmin diagram and a fallacy list judge the same sentence by different tests, so they will rate its strength differently without any file being wrong.
- The slips in finding 9 and the CM1-01 mismatch may be drafting errors that arose because the article has no item IDs, so each file had to invent its own locators. This would explain why the errors are about location and not about substance.
- The close agreement among the files may be partly produced by a shared reading of the article, because they were run on one text with the same brief. If so, agreement is weaker confirmation than it appears.
- Finding 3 may reflect DM-07 using "longer tier" loosely for "the later tiers", which would make its sentence about the medium tier correct and its mention of L45 a slip.

# Toulmin analysis of the adoption measurement article

The article is "Adopt an AI, today: a workaround for measuring AI transformation". The material has no paragraph or section IDs, so each part is referred to by its heading or by quoted text. I identified five arguments that carry the article's point of view and labelled each one: claim (C), ground (G), warrant (W), backing (B), rebuttal (R) and qualifier (Q). Where the author gives no text for a part, the diagram says "not stated" and does not fill the gap with a guess. A warrant marked "implied" is one the ground needs in order to reach the claim, and I say how I derived it.

## Argument 1: organisations measure by adoption because it is countable early

```
G   "Neither shows up quickly in financial results, and few organisations can trace either back to AI specifically."
      (value in the form boards and executives want is slow and hard to attribute)
W   (implied) When the preferred measure is unavailable, organisations report whatever
      can be counted early. The author does not state this.
B   Not stated. The text gives no survey, case or source.
Q   "Adoption seems to have gone mainstream as the way organisations describe their progress with AI"
      ("seems" is the only hedge)
R   Not stated. No organisation that measures differently is mentioned.
C   "So AI programs report adoption instead, because it can be counted from the first week of a rollout."
```

Finding: the ground and the claim are both plausible and consistent with each other. The ground describes one cause (value is slow to show), the claim names that cause as the reason. The unstated warrant is a general rule about organisational behaviour with no backing. The sentence "Following their lead, vendors set their pricing based on seats and usage, and consultancies build their frameworks around it" adds a causal direction (programs lead, vendors follow) that has no ground. The opposite direction, where vendor pricing makes seat and usage data the easiest thing to report, is equally compatible with the text.

## Argument 2: adoption measures miss workarounds

```
G1  "A workaround does not show up as non-use."
G2  "The person still has the licence, still opens the tool and still counts as an active user, so on paper the tool has found a home."
G3  Five examples by level (interface, task, workflow, team, leadership), closed by
      "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation."
W   (stated in part) "If adoption means anything at work, it means the tool works well enough, as designed, for people to get the job done with it. A workaround is its opposite."
      Implied step: a usage measure is therefore inadequate if it cannot tell the two apart.
B   The statement about "actual observations from research" is the only backing, and it names no study, sample or date.
Q   "Faced with any tool at work, a person does one of two things. They use it as designed, or they find a workaround that gets the job done."
      This is an absolute statement. It is not a qualifier, and it removes partial or mixed use from consideration.
R   Not stated. The article does not consider that usage data could be read alongside other signals (support requests, task completion, time per task).
C   Usage-based adoption figures cannot show whether a tool is used as designed or worked around.
```

Finding: this is the strongest argument in the article, because G1 and G2 follow from how usage counting works (a counted log-in does not record what happens afterwards). The weak points are these. First, the examples in G3 show that workarounds can exist, but not how common they are, so the claim that workarounds are a large blind spot has no frequency evidence. Second, the backing is a bare assertion of research. Third, the two-way split in the qualifier position is stated as fact and leaves out use that is partly as designed and partly not. Fourth, the Team example (opening the tool daily so usage is recorded) and the Leadership example (recording enough usage to stay compliant, but not enough to suggest a smaller team) are cases of gaming the metric, which is a different problem from a design workaround. The article groups them under one heading.

## Argument 3: adoption cannot record value that removes the need for work

```
G   Two examples: documents that update automatically so "nobody has to request them, process the request or answer the follow-up call", and a product built so that "the team that checked for that error has nothing left to check."
W   (implied) A usage measure can only register value where AI use increases or where
      a before-and-after comparison of the same work exists.
      The text supports this in part: "nothing in it is being used more than it was before, in fact there is no earlier version of the work to compare it with."
B   Not stated. The examples are hypothetical ("If a customer's documents update...", "If a product is built...").
Q   "some of the most valuable changes" (a partial claim, correctly limited)
R   Not stated.
C   "An adoption measure has no way to record this value."
```

Finding: the argument is valid for usage counts as defined in the article. The ground is hypothetical, so what it shows is that such value is possible, not that it is among the most valuable changes. The claim also cuts against the article's own remedy. The medium-term tier asks the program to "track time, quality, errors, and the experience of staff and customers for each piece of work the program changes, compared with how it was done before", and Argument 3 says removed work has no earlier version to compare. Only the end-state tier ("including work that is no longer needed") addresses it, and that tier is a plan to be tested through small trials, not a measure.

## Argument 4: nobody adopts AI, so adoption is the wrong concept

```
G1  Two cases: a person uses a tool with AI built in, or a person learns a new job because agents now do part of the work.
G2  Analogies: "Nobody describes booking a flight online as adopting ecommerce, or describes a new project management app as adopting the cloud." Web search "followed this path."
W   (implied) If a technology becomes a component of other tools, or if what people do is
      learn a job, then "adopting" that technology is not a real activity, and a program organised around it is mis-specified.
B   The web search history (late 1990s query syntax, now a search box). It is one example and it is given as a pattern, not sourced.
Q   "Taken literally, they do not."  (a qualifier by the word "literally")
R   Not stated. A rebuttal is available: adoption is a normal term for organisation-level
      change (for example, adopting a new system), and the author's own title uses it.
C   "AI adoption assumes that people actually "adopt AI". Taken literally, they do not."
```

Finding: this is the weakest link in the chain, because the warrant depends on a literal reading of a term that practitioners use loosely. The two-case split in G1 is stated as complete ("what people do with those tools falls into two cases") with no argument that other cases do not exist, for example a person who chooses a standalone AI assistant and takes responsibility for its output. That case is exactly the one the article's opening sentence says does not exist ("AI is not a single thing that a person chooses and takes responsibility for"), and the article gives no ground for that. The analogies establish that other technologies lost the label as they became ordinary, but they do not show that AI is on the same path. The sentence "A program built around adopting AI is organised around a technology that is becoming a component of everything" predicts this without evidence. The article's own title and its closing phrase "bringing the AI home" use the language it argues against.

## Argument 5: workarounds show design failure, not resistance

```
G1  "People build workarounds because they are responsible for getting the work done and the tool as designed did not let them do it."
G2  "When an adoption does not work out, the common explanations are that staff are resisting, that leaders are not engaged enough, or that the organisation did not follow the program."
W   (stated) "Each explanation attributes the failure to people. None of them questions the measures the program used or the design of the tools it introduced."
      Implied step: if a failure can be located in design, locating it in people is an error.
B   Not stated. No example is given of a program that blamed people when design was the cause.
Q   "Treating it as resistance discards that information." and "Training people to use the tool as designed will not help when the design is the reason they work around it."
      The second sentence is conditional ("when the design is the reason"), which is a proper limit.
R   Not stated. The article does not allow that some workarounds come from resistance, skill gaps or
      gaming of the metric (its own Team and Leadership examples).
C   "Each workaround shows where the design failed" (the section heading), supported by "A program measured by adoption rates cannot see workarounds, so when the work does not improve it has no evidence about the design and looks for the cause in people instead."
```

Finding: the heading claims every workaround shows a design failure. The article's own Team and Leadership examples (no time for training, a manager shaping usage figures) are failures of workload and incentives, and the remedy it gives for them ("time to learn", "a clear statement of how adoption figures will and will not be used") is not a design change to the tool. The claim therefore needs the qualifier "design in the broad sense, including work organisation", which the article does not state. The list of common explanations in G2 is asserted without a source, and the claim that organisations reach for people-based causes because they lack design evidence is a causal story with no case behind it.

## Argument 6: report value in tiers, starting with workarounds

```
G   "A program still needs early evidence, because the value of AI takes time to show up in the numbers."
W   (implied) Evidence about workarounds is early, collectable and a valid proxy for later value.
      This is not argued. The text says only that "Workarounds found and removed can be reported from the first weeks of a rollout."
B   "Each comes from established practice in building valuable solutions: observe how the work is really done, design for the result rather than the tool, make sure people can do what is asked of them, and start from a clear picture of what is being built."
      No source is given for "established practice".
Q   "it can report value in tiers" ("can", a permissive claim, not a necessity)
R   Not stated. Costs of observing work and interviewing staff are not considered, nor the risk that workaround counts become another target that people manage.
C   An AI program should replace a single usage figure with tiered reporting: short term (tools work as designed), medium term (work is better), longer term (people can do new jobs), end state (the intended future is reached).
```

Finding: the claim follows from Arguments 2 and 5 only if workarounds are common and reliably observed. The warrant that a count of workarounds removed is evidence of value is the unstated step that carries the weight. Fewer workarounds may mean a better tool, or may mean staff have learned not to disclose them, which is the same pattern the article describes for usage figures. The backing is an appeal to what is "obvious" ("One look at that list, and it's obvious: none of these tiers is new"), which is a reason the proposal is low risk, not a reason it works.

## Overall reading of the diagrams

| Argument | Ground quality | Warrant | Likely point of error |
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
| 1 Adoption reported because countable | Plausible, unsourced | Implied, general rule | Causal direction of vendors and programs |
| 2 Adoption misses workarounds | Strong (how counting works) | Partly stated | Frequency of workarounds not shown; backing is a bare assertion of research |
| 3 Adoption misses removed work | Hypothetical examples | Implied | Conflicts with the medium-term tier of the remedy |
| 4 Nobody adopts AI | Analogies | Implied, literal reading | Complete two-case split, and the target term used loosely by practitioners |
| 5 Workarounds show design failure | Assertion | Stated | Heading is wider than the evidence; Team and Leadership examples are not design faults |
| 6 Tiered reporting | General appeal | Implied | Workaround counts treated as a valid early proxy for value |

On the brief's first question, the diagnosis of the phenomenon (adoption is counted, and counts cannot see workarounds or removed work) is supported at the level of logic: the limits of a usage count follow from what it records. The material does not show how widely organisations rely on adoption or how often workarounds occur, so those parts are asserted. On the second question, the point of view is valid where it states what a usage measure cannot show, and weaker where it moves from there to a reason for every failure (Argument 5), to a rejection of the concept (Argument 4), and to a remedy (Argument 6). What it leaves out is evidence of prevalence, any rebuttal, and the possibility that the proposed measures have the same blind spots.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The technique assumes the text is one argument chain that can be split into parts. I split it into six arguments by topic, and a different split (for example one argument with sub-claims) would give different diagrams.
- Warrants marked "implied" are my reconstruction of the step needed to connect ground to claim. The author did not write them, and the author may hold different ones. I tried to keep them to the minimum the ground requires.
- The material is one article with no sources, no date and no publisher, and its text was supplied because the page could not be fetched. The technique can show what the argument rests on, but it cannot check whether the "actual observations from research" exist or whether the examples are typical.
- The technique labels structure. It does not measure how common workarounds are or whether adoption figures are as dominant as claimed. The material cannot answer either.
- Rebuttals are mostly "not stated" because the article contains no counter-argument. The rebuttals I note in Arguments 4 and 5 are my additions and are marked as such.

## Alternative explanations

- The main finding is that the article's diagnosis is logically sound but its prevalence claims and its wider conclusions are unsupported. Another reading is that the article is not trying to prove prevalence. It describes itself as a workaround and draws on research the author has done, so its aim may be to give practitioners a framework to look with, and the missing backing reflects genre (a short opinion piece) and not weak reasoning.
- The gap between the heading of Argument 5 and its examples may be a difference of definition. If "design" covers work organisation, incentives and training time, as it does in the author's WX idea ("which steps people do and which steps are automated, what context passes at each handover"), then the Team and Leadership examples are design failures and the claim holds. The apparent error would then be a definitional choice that the article does not state.
- The tension between Argument 3 and the medium-term tier may be deliberate sequencing. The author may mean that removed work is handled only in the end-state tier, and that the tiers are cumulative, so there is no contradiction.

# Fallacy analysis of "Adopt an AI, today: a workaround for measuring AI transformation"

The material carries no item IDs, so passages are referred to by the article's own section headings (opening, "People use tools and learn new jobs", "People use a tool as designed or work around it", "Workarounds happen at every level, from the interface to team leadership", "Each workaround shows where the design failed", "What an AI program should measure and do instead"). Quotations are copied exactly from the article.

Every entry below is a prompt for missing support. None is proof that the claim is false.

## Argument in explicit form

The article does not set out premises and conclusion separately, so the reconstruction below is mine and is the basis for the entries that follow.

- P1. Value from AI is slow to appear in financial results, so programs report adoption, which can be counted early.
- P2. Adoption counts use. Use and effective work can differ, and a workaround still registers as use.
- P3. Some of the most valuable changes remove work, so there is nothing to count as use.
- P4. Adoption assumes people "adopt AI", but people only use tools with AI inside them or learn new jobs.
- P5. People work around tools because the design failed, and programs that cannot see workarounds blame people.
- C1 (diagnosis). Adoption measures miss workarounds and value.
- C2 (point of view). Programs should measure workarounds, then work quality, then new jobs, then progress to an end state.

## Suspected defects

### 1. Unsupported general claim about what organisations do (opening)

- Passage: "Boards mostly point AI at cost reduction and customer service, and executives report productivity gains." The opening also says adoption "seems to have gone mainstream".
- Pattern or rule: hasty generalisation, and breach of the pragma-dialectical burden of proof rule (a standpoint that is put forward must be defended when challenged).
- Missing support: any survey, case or named source showing what boards and executives mostly do, or how widely adoption is used as the progress measure. P1 is the starting point of the diagnosis, so C1 depends on it.

### 2. Causal order asserted without evidence (opening)

- Passage: "Following their lead, vendors set their pricing based on seats and usage, and consultancies build their frameworks around it."
- Pattern or rule: possible questionable cause (the order of influence is assumed).
- Missing support: evidence that vendor pricing and consultancy frameworks followed programs rather than the reverse, or arose independently. The article does not need this claim for C1, so its effect is on credibility, not on the logic.

### 3. Evidence announced but not provided (workarounds at every level)

- Passage: "These are actual observations from research on tools and agentic automation."
- Pattern or rule: appeal to unnamed authority, and breach of the burden of proof rule.
- Missing support: the research, its sample, its setting and how often each workaround was seen. The five-level typology and the task example ("Staff who see the review as unnecessary change details in the underlying records so that the case no longer triggers it...") rest on this sentence alone. The material cannot show whether the observations are real or how common they are.

### 4. Possibility presented as the usual case (adoption problems list)

- Passage: "Use and effective work can move in opposite directions." The support is one illustration of a person needing ten attempts.
- Pattern or rule: hasty generalisation from a constructed instance.
- Missing support: evidence of how often usage and effective work diverge. The claim that a divergence can occur is supported. The diagnosis needs it to occur often enough to make adoption measures misleading, and the article does not say how often.

### 5. Straw man on the meaning of "adopt" (People use tools and learn new jobs)

- Passage: "AI adoption assumes that people actually "adopt AI". Taken literally, they do not." The article then argues "Nobody describes booking a flight online as adopting ecommerce, or describes a new project management app as adopting the cloud."
- Pattern or rule: straw man (a literal reading is attacked that adoption programs may not hold), with a universal claim ("Nobody") and an analogy.
- Missing support: a showing that adoption measures depend on the literal reading, and evidence that the ecommerce and cloud comparisons are close enough to AI. The article itself describes adoption as "borrowed from earlier software rollouts, where success meant getting people to use the new system", which suggests the term is used in an ordinary organisational sense, not a literal one. The article's own point stands without this step, because the two-case typology does not need the word to be literally wrong.

### 6. Analogy and extrapolation from web search (People use tools and learn new jobs)

- Passage: "Web search followed this path." and "A program built around adopting AI is organised around a technology that is becoming a component of everything."
- Pattern or rule: false analogy and prediction stated as present fact.
- Missing support: reasons to expect AI to follow search, and evidence that it already has. The second case in the typology (a person who "is learning a job, with new tasks, judgements and accountabilities") is not a component that is becoming ordinary, so the claim covers only the first case.

### 7. Two-option split that leaves out other cases (As designed or workaround)

- Passage: "Faced with any tool at work, a person does one of two things. They use it as designed, or they find a workaround that gets the job done." The article adds "A workaround is its opposite."
- Pattern or rule: false dilemma, and a definition that is stipulated and then relied on (see entry 8).
- Missing support: treatment of mixed use, partial use, genuine non-use, and use that is neither as designed nor a workaround that gets the job done. Genuine non-use matters because the article's own claim is that a workaround "does not show up as non-use", which implies non-use is something usage figures do detect.

### 8. Circular definition of adoption (As designed or workaround)

- Passage: "If adoption means anything at work, it means the tool works well enough, as designed, for people to get the job done with it."
- Pattern or rule: begging the question (the conclusion is built into the definition).
- Missing support: a reason to define adoption this way rather than as use. If adoption is defined to exclude workarounds, then it follows that counting use cannot measure it, so C1 on this point is true by definition. The factual part, that a person with a licence who opens the tool still counts as an active user, is separately sound (see the passages not flagged).

### 9. Sweeping claim that every workaround shows design failure (Each workaround shows where the design failed)

- Passage: "Each workaround shows which part of the design failed, for whom, and what people do instead."
- Pattern or rule: hasty generalisation, and an inconsistency with the article's own cases.
- Missing support: the article's team example (no time for training, so the team opens the tool each day to record usage) and its leadership example (a manager keeps recorded usage low enough to protect the team) are caused by workload and incentives. The remedies given for them are training time and a statement about how figures will be used, not a change to the tool. The claim fits the interface, task and workflow cases better than the team and leadership cases.

### 10. Blanket claim about how failures are explained (Each workaround shows where the design failed)

- Passage: "Each explanation attributes the failure to people. None of them questions the measures the program used or the design of the tools it introduced." The article continues "so when the work does not improve it has no evidence about the design and looks for the cause in people instead."
- Pattern or rule: straw man and false dichotomy between people and design, plus an unsupported causal claim about how programs behave.
- Missing support: evidence of how programs actually explain failure. "The organisation did not follow the program" is arguably a claim about the program, not about people. The leadership example in the article itself locates a cause in a person's choice, so the article does not treat person-level causes as always wrong.

### 11. Tension between two statements about measuring value (opening and The largest gap)

- Passage: the opening says "few organisations can trace either back to AI specifically", while a later section says "When AI speeds up the steps of an existing process, the gain can be measured".
- Pattern or rule: inconsistency between premises.
- Missing support: an account of when attribution to AI is possible. The two statements may be reconcilable (measuring a gain differs from attributing it to AI), but the article does not say so.

### 12. Superlative and unclear claim about value that removes work (The largest gap)

- Passage: "The largest gap is value that adoption cannot see at all." and "AI may be part of how either change works, but nothing in it is being used more than it was before, in fact there is no earlier version of the work to compare it with."
- Pattern or rule: unsupported comparison, plus a premise that is hard to follow.
- Missing support: a comparison showing this gap is larger than the others, and evidence beyond two hypothetical cases. If AI is part of how the change works, it is in use, so the statement that nothing is "being used more than it was before" needs explaining. The conclusion that removed work cannot be recorded as use is plausible for the examples given, but the claim of size is not supported.

### 13. The proposed replacement may share the flaw it criticises (What an AI program should measure)

- Passage: "Workarounds found and removed can be reported from the first weeks of a rollout, which is when adoption figures are reported now." The method is "Observe the work as it is done, ask people what they do when a tool does not give them what they need".
- Pattern or rule: double standard (a proxy is faulted for being easy to report, then a new reportable proxy is offered), and a possible gap in the premises about concealment.
- Missing support: why a count of workarounds found is a better indicator than a count of use, and how observation and questioning would reach workarounds that the article says people hide (the team and leadership examples). Neither the article nor the material gives evidence that the tiers have worked in practice.

### 14. Appeal to established practice (closing paragraph)

- Passage: "One look at that list, and it's obvious: none of these tiers is new." and "we've done this before with methods that still work".
- Pattern or rule: appeal to tradition or common practice, and an appeal to obviousness in place of support.
- Missing support: evidence that the older methods worked for the kinds of change the article describes, given its own statement that "AI is changing work in ways that are hard to picture in advance." The closing also does not explain why programs use adoption if the better methods are well known. The article's answer (adoption is borrowed from earlier software rollouts) is given, but it is not tested.

### 15. Workers assumed to be right (Task workarounds and the fix list)

- Passage: "Task workarounds need checks that ask for real judgement, not approval." This follows the task example in which staff edit records so a review is not triggered.
- Pattern or rule: assumption that the person working around the tool has judged correctly (a form of begging the question).
- Missing support: a way to tell a workaround that exposes a poor review step from one that removes a needed control. The article's premise is that people "are responsible for getting the work done", which does not show they judge the review correctly.

## Passages checked and not flagged

- A person who keeps a licence, opens the tool and still works the old way will count as an active user ("A workaround does not show up as non-use"). The conclusion follows from how usage is counted, so no fallacy is suspected in the logic. The frequency of this behaviour is a separate matter (entries 3 and 4).
- The statement that usage figures "cannot show what makes an app or agent useful" follows from what usage figures contain.
- The claim that value from removed work has no earlier version to compare with is coherent for the two examples given, apart from the points in entry 12.
- The closing remark that adoption "is itself a workaround" is a deliberate extension of the article's own term and is not flagged as a defect in reasoning, although it stretches the earlier definition.

## What the entries show

The narrow diagnosis, that usage counts cannot distinguish designed use from workarounds or capture work that no longer exists, follows from how usage is counted. The weaker parts are the empirical premises (entries 1, 3, 4), the definition and typology steps (entries 5, 7, 8, 9), and the proposed solution (entries 13, 14). The argument leaves out evidence of prevalence, evidence that the proposed tiers work, and the cases (non-use, partial use, useful workarounds) that do not fit its two options.

## Assumptions and limitations

- The article is not written as premises and conclusion, so the technique's minimum requirement was met only through my reconstruction. A different reconstruction could change which entries apply.
- The technique checks the form of the argument against known defect patterns. It cannot test whether the article's factual claims are true, and the material holds nothing outside the article to test them against.
- The article is a position piece on a general-audience platform. Missing citations may be a feature of the genre and not a sign of weak reasoning, and the publisher and date are not given.
- Labels were applied only where a passage and a gap in support could both be pointed to. Some entries (2, 5, 6) are weaker than others and are closer to questions than to defects.
- No counting or text analysis was called for, so no code was run.

## Alternative explanations

- The many missing-support entries may reflect the genre, not weak reasoning. A practitioner essay that argues for a way of thinking can reasonably rely on plausible examples, and the core claim (a usage count cannot see a workaround) needs only possibility, not prevalence. On this reading the empirical gaps matter less than entries 1, 3 and 4 suggest.
- The straw man and false dilemma entries (5, 7, 10) may be deliberate simplification for a typology, where two cases are a teaching device and not a claim that nothing else exists. The article does not say this, so the reader cannot tell which it is.
- The tension in entries 9 and 11 may come from the article using "design" and "measure" in a wide sense that includes workload and incentives. If so, the claim "each workaround shows where the design failed" would be consistent, but only with a wider meaning of design than the article states.
